title: Solve 2 step equations

findings.finding: Keep the equation fixed while varying the proposed solution.
findings.breakdown: The run highlights that verification tests the supplied value against both sides of the equation.
findings.checked: The existing practice changes the equation between parts. Substitution and comparison are taught in p6-verifying-solutions. All proposed calculations are correct.
findings.assumptions: Uses only substitution and arithmetic already required in this topic.

repair.proposal: Append parts k–o under the existing instruction. Add one line: “Predict each result before checking.” (k) x=3, 2x+5=3x: No; LHS=11, RHS=9. (l) x=4, 2x+5=3x: No; LHS=13, RHS=12. (m) x=5, 2x+5=3x: Yes; both sides equal 15. (n) x=6, 2x+5=3x: No; LHS=17, RHS=18. Follow with unpatterned (o) x=−2, 2x+5=3x: No; LHS=1, RHS=−6.

findings.doneWhen: The appended run varies only the supplied value and ends with an unpatterned check.

findings.finding: Extend the existing equivalent-equation chain by constructing an equation with the same solution.
findings.breakdown: Students use the solution found in part b to construct and connect another equivalent equation.
findings.checked: Part b gives x=7. Consequently 4x−5=23. Every operation in the proposed chain is taught in p14-example and p15-examples-block and is reversible.
findings.assumptions: An optional follow-up using only methods available by the end of equivalent-equations.

repair.proposal: After part b append: (c) Complete 4x−5=___ so that it is equivalent to 5x−3=32. Answer: 23. (d) Starting with x+2=9, show a chain of equivalent equations ending with 4x−5=23. Expected chain: x+2=9 → x=7 → 4x=28 → 4x−5=23, applying −2, ×4 and −5 to both sides.

findings.doneWhen: Each added part asks one question and uses the existing solution and transformation methods.

findings.finding: Equations combining multiplication and division on the unknown precede the explanation of how to handle that form.
findings.breakdown: The preparation models one multiplicative operation together with addition or subtraction. In 3x/2=9, students must instead organise two multiplicative operations. The stated two-step procedure does not explain this variant; the explicit preparation comes later in question 11.
findings.checked: Checked p15-examples-block, p22-identify, p25-guided-practice, p32-identify, p33-identify and p34-example-group. These teach the component operations but do not model their combined use in ax/b=c. p39-q11-content explicitly supplies the missing interpretation and starting operations.
findings.assumptions: Students know the individual inverse operations. The issue is recognising the new combined form, independent of calculator use.

repair.proposal: Move p39-q11-content's introductory explanation and parts a and b immediately before p36-q4. Leave part c later, repeating its equation if needed so it remains self-contained.

findings.doneWhen: Before p36-q4, students have interpreted ax/b as two operations and practised solving it by multiplying first and by dividing first.

findings.finding: Extend the grouping comparison by using each equation's solution in the other equation.
findings.breakdown: Changing the right-hand side makes the effect of the fraction bar's grouping concrete.
findings.checked: Part a has solution a=6 and part b has solution a=16. Substitution gives 16/3+5=31/3 and (6+5)/3=11/3. Substitution is taught at the beginning of the booklet.
findings.assumptions: An optional numerical follow-up requiring only previously taught substitution and fraction arithmetic.

repair.proposal: After part c append: (d) In part a, replace 7 with a number so that a=16 is the solution. Answer: 31/3. (e) In part b, replace 7 with a number so that a=6 is the solution. Answer: 11/3.

findings.doneWhen: The two added parts retain the existing expressions and change only their right-hand sides.

findings.finding: The practice moves directly to several nested outer operations around a grouped numerator.
findings.breakdown: Earlier questions separately practise a grouped numerator with an inner coefficient and a fractional variable term with an outside constant. Part j combines these with an outside multiplier and subtraction, requiring five inverse operations. No preceding question bridges that combination.
findings.checked: p48-information-steps supplies the general reverse-order method. p63-t, p63-u and p64-q3-g practise grouped numerators; p62-q2-n and p64-q3-a practise outside constants. None combines an outside constant with the grouped numerator before j adds the further multiplier. The closing challenge is therefore preceded by a sharp rise rather than a gradual build.
findings.assumptions: Students can perform the individual operations; calculator availability does not resolve the coordination demand.

repair.proposal: Immediately before p64-q3-j insert: “Solve (2x+9)/4−5=7.” Answer: x=19. This adds an outside subtraction to the previously practised grouped fraction. Part j then adds just the outside multiplier.

findings.doneWhen: Students encounter a grouped numerator with an outside constant before coordinating both an outside multiplier and constant in parts j and k.

findings.finding: Extend parts j and k by constructing another equation that clears to the same intermediate equation.
findings.breakdown: Students connect the shared solution to the fixed product obtained when clearing the denominator.
findings.checked: Both existing parts clear to x−6=90. The added equation 15=(x−6)/6 also gives x=96; with x=96, 10=(x−6)/9. All methods are available by this topic.
findings.assumptions: An optional follow-up to the existing numerical comparison.

repair.proposal: Immediately after part k add optional follow-up parts: (i) Solve 15=(x−6)/6. Answer: x=96. (ii) Complete 10=(x−6)/□ so that its solution is x=96. Answer: 9. (iii) Explain why these equations and parts j and k have the same solution. Expected answer: multiplying each equation by its denominator gives x−6=90.

findings.doneWhen: Each follow-up part asks one question and connects directly to the existing equations.

findings.finding: The example substitutes 0.6 dollars for the given 60 cents without writing the conversion.
findings.breakdown: Constructing the equation requires choosing a common currency unit. Defining c in dollars identifies that unit but does not explicitly connect the given 60 cents to the new value 0.6.
findings.checked: The question supplies 60 cents, while the equation uses 0.6. No preceding line states the conversion. The guided purchase problem uses prices already expressed in dollars.
findings.assumptions: Students know dollars and cents; the missing cue models applying that knowledge when constructing the equation. No calculator assumption is needed.

repair.proposal: Immediately before the equation add: “Use dollars throughout: 60 cents = $0.60.”

findings.doneWhen: The worked example explicitly connects the given price to the value substituted into its equation.

findings.finding: The practice moves from linear inspection directly to finding two values satisfying a product of two variable expressions.
findings.breakdown: Students must now coordinate t and 10−t, generate suitable factor pairs and find two solutions. The preceding linear and grouped questions do not build towards that combination.
findings.checked: Checked p9 teaching and p10–p12 practice. p10-q1-h repeats the unknown additively; p11-q6 introduces grouping but retains linear inspection. Earlier substitution teaching supports checking candidates, not generating them. The harder-question label does not supply the missing bridge.
findings.assumptions: Elementary multiplication facts are available. No calculator or quadratic-solving method is assumed.

repair.proposal: Add: “The factors t and 10−t add to 10. List the positive whole-number factor pairs of 21. Which pair adds to 10? Try each member of that pair as t and check.” Expected values: t=3 and t=7.

findings.doneWhen: Students have a route to generate both values while still choosing the factor pair and verifying each value.

findings.finding: The general equivalence rule omits the nonzero restriction on multiplication and division.
findings.breakdown: Following the written rule, multiplying x+1=4 by zero produces 0=0, which admits every value rather than preserving the original solution x=3.
findings.checked: The investigation, balance demonstrations, examples and summaries consistently use valid nonzero operations but never state the restriction. Those examples do not expose why multiplying by zero fails.
findings.assumptions: The stated equivalence rule is intended to guide students' transformations of equations.

repair.proposal: Qualify the summaries: “Adding or subtracting the same quantity on both sides, or multiplying or dividing both sides by the same nonzero number, gives an equivalent equation.” Beside the multiplication/division teaching add: “Multiplying by zero loses the original condition; division by zero is undefined.”

findings.doneWhen: The general rule and its summaries consistently state the nonzero restriction.

findings.finding: The topic lacks a review of combining like terms and solving two-step equations, both used directly in its worked examples.
findings.breakdown: Adam's example simplifies a+(a+1) before solving; Asher's example solves 12n+50=410. Students must recall these substantial procedures while learning contextual modelling.
findings.checked: Earlier teaching supplies both methods. The immediately preceding topic reviews expression translation and practises writing equations, but does not rehearse simplification or two-step solving. The proposed review is short, mathematically correct and fits within one page.
findings.assumptions: The teacher checks the review and responds to gaps before teaching contextual modelling.

repair.proposal: Before p71-method add: “Simplify: (a) x+(x+1), (b) x+(x−3), (c) 3x+2x+4. Solve: (d) 2x+1=19, (e) 5x+20=80, (f) 3x−4=17.” Expected answers: 2x+1; 2x−3; 5x+4; x=9; x=12; x=7.

findings.doneWhen: The teacher can check recall of combining like terms and the relevant two-step solving procedures before modelling begins.

findings.finding: The exercise requires interpreting complete cancellation of the variable as every value being a solution, but preceding teaching does not model that interpretation.
findings.breakdown: In 2x+37+4-2x=41, combining like terms gives 41=41. The taught isolation procedure cannot produce x equal to a number. Students need to recognise that this true equality places no restriction on x; otherwise they may report no solution or choose an arbitrary single value.
findings.checked: Reviewed all supplied teaching. p4-identify-e includes x+3=3+x, and its supplied answer states that it is true for every x, but the student task only identifies whether it is an equation. It does not demonstrate interpreting cancellation while solving. p5-solutions and p6-verifying-solutions establish truth and substitution; p25-solving and p34-example-group model isolating x. None connects a simplified equality with no remaining variable to every value satisfying the original equation. Independently simplifying the target confirms 41=41, with no domain restrictions.
findings.assumptions: Combining like terms is assumed prior algebra knowledge. Interpreting complete cancellation is a new solving outcome within this topic. Calculator availability does not affect the finding.

repair.proposal: Beside p39-q10-e, add a brief explanation: combining like terms gives 41=41; this is true whatever real value x takes, so every real value is a solution.

findings.doneWhen: Teaching explicitly connects cancellation to a true numerical equality and explains why every real value satisfies the original equation.
